extracted.intended_audience: monarchs, governors, learned gentlemen and educated readers (addressed 'To the King')
extracted.subtask_description: A classical early-modern essay (Francis Bacon) arguing for the public and private benefits of learning, illustrated by historical examples and practical consequences for rulers, soldiers, and citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repressing social inconveniences (maintaining society and peace)
rubrics_metrics.description: “That other merit of learning, in repressing the inconveniences which grow from man to man...” (learning restrains savage and unreclaimed desires and maintains society).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via the Orpheus’ theatre allegory: when people 'give ear to precepts, to laws, to religion, sweetly touched with eloquence and persuasion of books, of sermons, of harangues, so long is society and peace maintained'; if these instruments be silent, 'all things dissolve into anarchy and confusion.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Relieving necessities arising from nature (practical/technological benefits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning relieves the necessities which arise from nature (practical inventions and remedies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as a distinct merit of learning alongside social benefits — learning supplies remedies to natural needs and practical problems (contrasted with repressing man-to-man inconveniences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learned rulers produce better times and governance
rubrics_metrics.description: “Under learned princes and governors there have been ever the best times” — learning in sovereigns correlates with prosperity and good government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guided by historical examples (Nerva, Trajan, Adrian, Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius, Queen Elizabeth) showing learned princes as patrons of learning, founders of libraries, promoters of peace, justice, and flourishing learning; learning gives rulers 'notions of religion, policy, and morality' that preserve them from excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning restrains rulers from ruinous and peremptory errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning supplies rulers with notions of religion, policy, and morality which 'do preserve them and refrain them from all ruinous and peremptory errors and excesses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learning functions as an internal check—'whispering evermore in their ears'—especially important when counsellors or servants are silent; illustrated by emperors who revered learning and thereby tempered their governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learned counsellors reason from substantial principles rather than mere experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Senators or counsellors who are learned 'proceed upon more safe and substantial principles, than counsellors which are only men of experience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The learned detect dangers earlier and base advice on principles; practical-only counsellors may fail to discover dangers until too late and then rely on quick wit rather than foresight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning enhances martial and military virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning has power and efficacy in enabling martial and military virtue and prowess (illustrated by Alexander the Great and Julius Caesar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Alexander educated by Aristotle, accompanied by learned men in camp; his judgments, metaphors, and strategic uses of rhetoric and speech are attributed to learning. Caesar's writings (Commentary), rhetorical acts, and calculated speeches show learning aiding command, strategy, and authority; Xenophon shows a philosopher acting effectively in war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning softens manners and mitigates barbarism (moral/private virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Emollit mores nec sinit esse feros” — learning takes away wildness and barbarism of minds and mitigates levity, temerity, and insolency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learning acquaints the mind to balance reasons, to examine doubts, and to 'accept of nothing but examined and tried'—it lessens vain admiration (root of weakness) and produces temperate dispositions; caveat that the accent must be on faithful/deep learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning mitigates fear of death and adverse fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Meditation upon mortality through learning 'taketh away or mitigateth fear of death or adverse fortune,' an impediment to virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by anecdotes (Epictetus' observations on mourning) and Virgil’s couplet: knowledge of causes leads to subjugation of fear and fate ('Quique metus omnes... Subjecit pedibus').

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning disposes the mind to growth and reformation (self-improvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning 'disposeth the constitution of the mind not to be fixed or settled in the defects thereof, but still to be capable and susceptible of growth and reformation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts learned and unlearned men: the unlearned hide faults and do not amend them; the learned intermix correction and amendment with use, enjoying the 'suavissima vita' of daily self-improvement ('indies sentire se fieri meliorem').

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge commands reason and belief — the highest form of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'commandment of knowledge' is a commandment over reason, belief, and understanding — higher than temporal or physical command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that knowledge sets up a 'throne' in the spirits and beliefs of men; those who command conscience or faith can exercise a powerful, enduring sovereignty (examples of heretics/impostors and the potency of conviction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning brings fortune and advancement to individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning gives fortune and advancement: 'Homer hath given more men their livings, than either Sylla, or Cæsar, or Augustus ever did.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim that learning provides livelihoods and advancement at scale; while arms and descent gain kingdoms, learning advances priesthood and other offices; historical observation about the social mobility and patronage enabled by letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning provides superior, inexhaustible pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures of the intellect/satisfaction of knowledge 'far surpasseth all other in nature' and yields no satiety—'no satiety, but satisfaction and appetite are perpetually interchangeable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasted with sensual or affective pleasures that fade; learning offers a stable, renewing delight and the pleasure of appreciating truth and seeing others' errors and labours from a secure vantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning secures immortality and continuance through writings
rubrics_metrics.description: Monuments of wit and learning are 'more durable than the monuments of power or of the hands' — letters pass through time like ships and make distant ages participate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Homer’s verses lasting centuries, printed images that 'generate still' and cast seeds in minds of others; books preserve and transmit thought beyond the life-span of physical monuments or originals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of faithful, deep learning (warning against superficial learning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The benefit of learning requires fidelity and depth: the accent 'fideliter' is needed, for 'a little superficial learning doth rather work a contrary effect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit caveat: shallow or partial knowledge may increase vanity or error rather than correct it. The essay repeatedly contrasts thorough, principled learning with superficial display or pretence.
